clips.hook: Latvia lost *30%* of its people. No war.
clips.title: Latvia lost 30% of its people. There was no war #Shorts
clips.desc: Japan is the famous shrinking country. It lost 3%. Latvia lost 30%.

clips.title: Why millions left Eastern Europe, in one number #Shorts
clips.desc: In 2000 a German produced 4x what a Bulgarian did.

clips.title: Bulgaria: two deaths for every birth #Shorts
clips.desc: And the census shows it's now the main reason the country is shrinking.

clips.hook: More people moved *in*. It still shrank.
clips.title: 35,000 more people moved in. Bulgaria still shrank #Shorts
clips.desc: Bulgaria 2025: migration turned positive, the population still fell.

shots.src: World Bank WDI · population (SP.POP.TOTL), change since 1990
shots.narration: Japan is the world's most famous shrinking country. {p} But on this chart, it barely moves. Since its peak in 2010, Japan has lost about three percent of its people. {p} Now look at Latvia. {pp} Since 1990, Latvia has lost thirty percent of its population. {p} Bulgaria, more than a quarter. {p} No war. No famine. No plague. {pp} So where did everyone go?

And Latvia isn't alone. {p} Here's every country in Europe, colored by how much its population has changed since 1990. {p} Green grew. Red shrank. {p} Ukraine's losses are mostly the war. But look at the red band running from the Baltic Sea down to the Balkans. {pp} Lithuania. Bulgaria. Bosnia. Albania. Each lost more than a fifth of its people. {p} Romania and Croatia, almost as much.

At its peak, Latvia had about two point six seven million people. {p} Today it has about one point eight six million. {p} That's around eight hundred thousand people gone, {pp} more than everyone who lives in the capital, Riga, today. {p} This is the story of Europe's vanishing countries: {p} why so many people left, why the numbers keep falling even now that people are coming back, <soft>and why the rest of Europe should be paying attention.</soft>

shots.src: World Bank WDI · fertility rate (births per woman)
shots.narration: It started with the end of the Soviet Union. {p} In 1991, Latvia, Lithuania and Estonia became independent again. Bulgaria and Romania had already thrown out their communist regimes two years earlier. {p} Freedom came with an economic collapse. Factories closed, savings vanished, prices exploded. {p} And people stopped having children. {p} In Latvia, births per woman fell from about two in 1990 to one point two five in 1995. {p} Bulgaria fell to almost exactly the same level.

shots.src: World Bank WDI · net migration as % of population, Latvia
shots.narration: Then the doors opened. {p} In 2004, the Baltic states joined the European Union. In 2007, Bulgaria and Romania followed. {p} Suddenly, a young Latvian could legally take a job in Dublin or London. Britain, Ireland and Sweden opened their job markets on day one. {p} When the 2008 financial crisis hit, Latvia's economy shrank by about a fifth. {pp} In 2010 alone, the country lost almost two percent of its population to emigration. {p} In a single year.

shots.src: World Bank WDI · net migration · Eurostat, EU citizens living in another EU country (2024)
shots.title: The great exit
shots.narration: Lithuania lost almost eighty thousand people to emigration in 2010 alone. {p} Romania, a much bigger country, lost about two point four million people to emigration between 1990 and 2024, by World Bank estimates. {p} Today, about three point one million Romanians live in other EU countries, mostly in Italy, Germany and Spain. {p} That's more than any other country in the EU.

items.text: 3.1 million Romanians in other EU countries

shots.src: World Bank WDI · GDP per capita, PPP (current international $)
shots.title: Output per person, 2000
shots.narration: Why did so many people leave? {p} Mostly, money. {p} In 2000, the average Bulgarian produced about six thousand four hundred dollars of value a year, adjusted for prices. {p} The average German? {pp} About twenty-seven thousand. More than four times as much. {p} When a bus ticket can quadruple your income, a lot of people buy the ticket.

shots.src: World Bank, ECA Economic Update: Migration and Brain Drain (Fall 2019)
shots.title: Who left
shots.narration: And the people who left weren't a random sample. {p} They were mostly young, in their twenties and thirties. {p} Many had a degree. {p} In other words, exactly the people who would have been raising the next generation of children at home. {pp} Emigration didn't just take people away. <soft>It took their future kids with them.</soft>

shots.src: World Bank WDI · population ages 65+ (% of total)
shots.narration: And the people who stayed got older. {p} In 1990, about one in eight Latvians was sixty-five or older. {p} Today, it's more than one in five. {p} In 1990, Latvia was younger than the EU average. Today, it has caught up. {p} Fewer young adults means fewer births, which means even fewer young adults twenty years later. {pp} It's a spiral, and it's very hard to get out of.

Quick favor: if you're finding this interesting, hit subscribe. It's free, and it's genuinely what keeps this channel going. {p} Now, here's the part most people miss. {pp} Today, emigration isn't the main reason these countries are shrinking.

shots.src: NSI Bulgaria, population and demographic processes 2025 (via Novinite, 29 Apr 2026) · CSB Latvia, population 2024 (via Baltic Times, 2025)
shots.title: Bulgaria, 2025
shots.narration: In 2025, Bulgaria recorded about fifty thousand births. {p} And almost a hundred thousand deaths. {pp} Two funerals for every baby. {p} Latvia's numbers look almost the same: in 2024, about thirteen thousand babies, and more than twenty-six thousand deaths.

shots.src: NSI Bulgaria, 2021 census final results (via Sofia Globe, 3 Oct 2022)
shots.title: Bulgaria lost 845,000 people, 2011–2021
shots.narration: Bulgaria's last census shows how the two forces compare. {p} Between 2011 and 2021, the country lost about eight hundred forty-five thousand people. {p} About three hundred forty-four thousand of them emigrated. {p} The other five hundred thousand or so were simply deaths outnumbering births. {pp} The biggest driver wasn't the airport anymore. <soft>It was the maternity ward, and the cemetery.</soft>

shots.src: World Bank WDI · life expectancy at birth, male · OECD/European Observatory, Latvia Country Health Profile 2023
shots.narration: And people in this region still die younger. {p} A Latvian man can expect to live about seventy-one and a half years. {p} The average man in the EU, seventy-nine. {p} Latvian women live almost ten years longer than Latvian men, the widest gap in the European Union. {p} Heart disease, heavy drinking and smoking hit men here especially hard.

shots.src: World Bank WDI · net migration as % of population, Lithuania · Statistics Lithuania via LRT (24 Feb 2023)
shots.narration: But here's the twist. {p} In 2019, for the first time in about three decades, more people moved to Lithuania than left it. {p} Estonia had already turned the corner a few years earlier, and lately Latvia and Bulgaria have had years like that too. {p} Some of the newcomers are Lithuanians coming home, from Britain, Norway and Germany. {p} Others are Ukrainians and Belarusians, many of them fleeing war and repression.

shots.src: World Bank WDI · GDP per capita, PPP, as % of the EU average
shots.narration: Part of the reason is that the money gap has shrunk. {p} In 2000, Lithuanians produced about thirty-eight percent as much per person as the EU average, adjusted for prices. {p} Today, it's about eighty-seven percent. {p} Latvia and Bulgaria have closed a big part of the gap too. {p} When home is almost as rich as abroad, {pp} <soft>coming back starts to make sense.</soft>

shots.src: NSI Bulgaria, population and demographic processes 2025 (via Novinite, 29 Apr 2026)
shots.title: Bulgaria, 2025
shots.narration: And yet, look at Bulgaria in 2025. {p} About forty-five thousand people moved in. Fewer than ten thousand left. {p} That's a gain of about thirty-five thousand people. {p} And the population still fell, by fourteen thousand. {pp} Because deaths outnumbered births by even more.

stats.label: more people moved in than left

shots.src: World Bank WDI · fertility rate (births per woman)
shots.narration: The deeper problem is the same one South Korea has. {p} Lithuania's fertility rate is now about one point one children per woman. Latvia's, about one point two. The EU as a whole is at about one point three. {p} To keep a population stable without immigration, you need about two point one. {p} Both are now among the lowest in the European Union.

Eurostat's baseline projection shows where this is heading. {p} By 2100, Latvia is projected to have about one point two million people. {p} That's more than a third fewer than today. {p} Lithuania, about one point eight million. {pp} Not gone. <soft>But a very different country.</soft>

None of this means Latvia or Bulgaria will disappear from the map. {p} But it does mean emptier villages, more schools closing, and fewer workers paying for more pensions. {p} And it's a preview. {pp} The European Union as a whole now has more deaths than births. {p} What hit the Baltics and the Balkans first, fast and loud, <soft>is coming more slowly for everyone else.</soft>

items.text: A preview for all of Europe

shots.narration: Not every country in the region took this path. {p} To see one that went a very different way, watch how Poland passed Japan. {p} I'm Chartbound. See you in the next one.

yt.title: Latvia Lost 30% of Its People. There Was No War.
yt.description:
Japan is the world's famous shrinking country, but it has lost about 3% of its people since its peak. Latvia has lost 30% since 1990. Bulgaria, more than a quarter. Why the Baltics and the Balkans emptied out, why emigration is no longer the main reason, why people are now coming back, and what the projections say.

Sources: World Bank WDI (SP.POP.TOTL, SP.DYN.TFRT.IN, SM.POP.NETM, NY.GDP.PCAP.PP.CD, NY.GDP.MKTP.KD, SP.POP.65UP.TO.ZS, SP.DYN.LE00.MA.IN/FE.IN, SP.DYN.CBRT.IN, SP.DYN.CDRT.IN); Eurostat proj_23np (EUROPOP2023); NSI Bulgaria (2025 data; 2021 census); CSB Latvia; Statistics Lithuania; Eurostat/European Parliament (EU movers 2024); World Bank ECA Economic Update: Migration and Brain Drain (2019); OECD/European Observatory, Latvia Country Health Profile 2023.
